claim: An account created on or after October 1, 2024 cannot create a launch configuration by any method (console, API, AWS CLI, or CloudFormation).
question: Can a new AWS account still create launch configurations?

values.display: cannot create new launch configurations using any method

qualifiers.scope: per account, by account creation date

evidence.quote: Accounts created on or after **October 1, 2024** cannot create new launch configurations using any method (console, API, AWS CLI, or CloudFormation).

note: FRESHNESS hypothesis confirmed on the page: blocked by any method for accounts created on or after 2024-10-01. Demand d39.

claim: An account created on or after June 1, 2023 cannot create a launch configuration in the console.
question: Since when can new accounts not create launch configurations in the console?

qualifiers.scope: per account, by account creation date

evidence.quote: Accounts created on or after **June 1, 2023** cannot create new launch configurations using the console.

claim: As of January 1, 2023, new EC2 instance types are not supported in launch configurations.
question: Do launch configurations support new EC2 instance types?

values.display: no longer supported in launch configurations

evidence.quote: As of **January 1, 2023**, new Amazon EC2 instance types are no longer supported in launch configurations.

claim: With a launch configuration you cannot create a group that launches both Spot and On-Demand Instances or that uses multiple instance types; those features need a launch template, which AWS recommends.
question: Which purchasing and instance-type features need a launch template instead of a launch configuration?

values.display: cannot create an Auto Scaling group that launches both Spot and On-Demand Instances or that specifies multiple instance types

evidence.quote: For example, you cannot create an Auto Scaling group that launches both Spot and On-Demand Instances or that specifies multiple instance types.
You must use a launch template to configure these features.
We recommend you use launch templates, which allow you to access the latest features and improvements.

claim: For Spot Instances in a mixed instances group, AWS recommends the price-capacity-optimized allocation strategy: it chooses the Spot pools that are least likely to be interrupted and have the lowest possible price.
question: Which Spot allocation strategy does AWS recommend for an Auto Scaling group?

values.display: least likely to be interrupted and have the lowest possible price

evidence.quote: The price and capacity optimized allocation strategy looks at both price and capacity to select the Spot Instance pools that are the least likely to be interrupted and have the lowest possible price.
We recommend this strategy when you're getting started.

| [New Spot allocation strategy](#DocumentHistory) | You can now use the price and capacity optimized allocation strategy to request Spot Instances from the Spot pools that are the least likely to be interrupted and have the lowest possible price. For more information, see [Allocation strategies](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/autoscaling/ec2/userguide/ec2-auto-scaling-mixed-instances-groups.html#allocation-strategies) in the *Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling User Guide*. | November 10, 2022 |

note: Added November 10, 2022 (history row). FRESHNESS: lowest-price was the old common answer; the page now marks it not recommended.

claim: AWS does not recommend the lowest-price Spot allocation strategy because it has the highest risk of interruption, and it is only available from the AWS CLI.
question: Why is the lowest-price Spot allocation strategy not recommended, and where can it be set?

values.display: only available when using the AWS CLI

qualifiers.scope: Spot allocation strategy of a mixed instances group

evidence.quote: We don't recommend the `lowest-price` strategy because it has the highest risk of interruption for your Spot Instances.
The `lowest-price` strategy is only available when using the AWS CLI.

note: Exam questions written before 2023 may still expect lowest-price as the cheapest answer.

claim: The capacity-optimized Spot allocation strategy launches into the pools with the most available capacity, using real-time capacity data, to reduce interruptions for workloads where restarting is expensive.
question: What does the capacity-optimized Spot allocation strategy optimize for?

evidence.quote: The `capacity-optimized` strategy automatically launches Spot Instances into the most available pools by looking at real-time capacity data and predicting which are the most available.
This helps to minimize possible disruptions for workloads that might have a higher cost of interruption associated with restarting work and checkpointing.

claim: With the prioritized On-Demand allocation strategy, put the instance type of your unused Reserved Instances first in the override list so the group launches it first and gets the Reserved Instance rate.
question: How can a mixed instances group use unused Reserved Instances?

values.display: discounted rate of the regular On-Demand Instance pricing applies if Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling launches matching instance types

evidence.quote: With Reserved Instances, your discounted rate of the regular On-Demand Instance pricing applies if Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling launches matching instance types.
When fulfilling On-Demand capacity, Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling determines which instance type to use first based on the order of instance types in the list of launch template overrides.

claim: Since November 18, 2025, the LaunchInstances API lets you request a specific number of instances in one Availability Zone synchronously and get immediate feedback on capacity, instead of waiting for asynchronous scaling.
question: What is synchronous provisioning in EC2 Auto Scaling, and when was it added?

evidence.quote: With synchronous provisioning, you use the LaunchInstances API to request a specific number of instances in a particular Availability Zone.
With asynchronous Auto Scaling, when you change the desired capacity or when a scaling policy triggers, Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling processes the scaling request and launches instances in the background.

| [Synchronous provisioning](#DocumentHistory) | You can now use the LaunchInstances API to synchronously launch instances with immediate feedback and have precise control over which Availability Zone instances launch in. For more information, see [Synchronous provisioning](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/autoscaling/ec2/userguide/launch-instances-synchronously). | November 18, 2025 |

note: Demand d59. GA 2025-11-18, before the exam cutoff of 2026-07-15, so examinable in principle; low exam frequency expected.

claim: The LaunchInstances API works only with groups that use launch templates; groups with launch configurations are not supported.
question: Does synchronous provisioning work with launch configurations?

values.display: only works with Auto Scaling groups that use launch templates

evidence.quote: The LaunchInstances API only works with Auto Scaling groups that use launch templates.
Auto Scaling groups that use launch configurations are not supported.

claim: A LaunchInstances call targets only one Availability Zone, and the API supports mixed instances policies that are fully On-Demand or fully Spot, not a mix of both.
question: What are the Availability Zone and purchasing limits of the LaunchInstances API?

values.display: can only target one Availability Zone
fully On-Demand or fully Spot purchasing options only

evidence.quote: Single AZ limitation per call – Each LaunchInstances API call can only target one Availability Zone, even if your Auto Scaling group spans multiple zones.
The LaunchInstances API supports mixed instances policies with fully On-Demand or fully Spot purchasing options only.

claim: An instance maintenance policy (added November 15, 2023) sets a minimum and maximum healthy percentage; the group replaces instances only within that range, so it can launch a new instance and wait for it to be ready before terminating the unhealthy one.
question: What does an instance maintenance policy control during instance replacement?

evidence.quote: You set the minimum and maximum healthy percentage parameters for the policy, and your Auto Scaling group can only increase and decrease capacity within that minimum-maximum range when replacing instances.
With an instance maintenance policy, you can make sure that Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling first launches a new instance and then waits for it to be fully ready before terminating the unhealthy instance.

| [Instance maintenance policies](#DocumentHistory) | You can now use an instance maintenance policy to define whether instances are launched before or after existing instances are terminated during events that cause your instances to be replaced, including an instance refresh. For more information, see [Instance maintenance policies](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/autoscaling/ec2/userguide/ec2-auto-scaling-instance-maintenance-policy.html) in the *Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling User Guide*. | November 15, 2023 |

claim: Since November 18, 2024, you can start a zonal shift on an Auto Scaling group: the group then launches all new capacity in the healthy Availability Zones and blocks scaling policies from decreasing desired capacity.
question: What does a zonal shift change in an Auto Scaling group, and when was it added?

values.display: launch all new capacity requests in the healthy Availability Zones
block scaling policies from decreasing desired capacity

evidence.quote: **Scaling out** – Auto Scaling will launch all new capacity requests in the healthy Availability Zones (`us-east-1b` and `us-east-1c`).
**Dynamic scaling** – Auto Scaling will block scaling policies from decreasing desired capacity in all Availability Zones.

| [Zonal shift](#DocumentHistory) | You can now use zonal shift to recover from application impairments in an Availability Zone. For more information, see [Auto Scaling group zonal shift](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/autoscaling/ec2/userguide/ec2-auto-scaling-zonal-shift.html).  | November 18, 2024 |

claim: Zonal shift is a capability of Amazon Application Recovery Controller (ARC); enabling it registers the Auto Scaling group with the ARC zonal shift service, and the group treats the shifted Availability Zone as impaired.
question: Which service provides zonal shift for an Auto Scaling group?

evidence.quote: Zonal shift is a capability in the Amazon Application Recovery Controller (ARC).
When you enable zonal shift for an Auto Scaling group, the group is registered with the ARC zonal shift service.

claim: For zonal shift, AWS recommends an instance maintenance policy with a minimum healthy percentage of 100, so the group waits for a new instance to be ready before it terminates an unhealthy one.
question: What instance maintenance policy does AWS recommend with zonal shift?

evidence.quote: Set an instance maintenance policy with a minimum healthy percentage of 100.
With this setting, Auto Scaling waits for a new instance to be ready to use before terminating an unhealthy instance.

claim: With the balanced best effort Availability Zone distribution, the group keeps an equal number of instances per enabled zone, but if launches fail in one zone it launches in another healthy zone; the distribution choice was added November 7, 2024.
question: What does the balanced best effort Availability Zone distribution strategy do when a launch fails in a zone?

values.display: attempts to launch instances in another healthy Availability Zone

evidence.quote: If launch attempts fail in an Availability Zone, Auto Scaling attempts to launch instances in another healthy Availability Zone.
This strategy is important for applications that need Availability Zone redundancy and are not impacted by imbalanced groups.

| [Availability Zone distribution](#DocumentHistory) | You can now choose an Availability Zone distribution for your Auto Scaling group. For more information, see [Auto Scaling group Availability Zone distribution](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/autoscaling/ec2/userguide/ec2-auto-scaling-availability-zone-balanced.html).  | November 7, 2024 |

note: Demand d18. The page does not say which strategy is the default; the hypothesis 'balanced best effort is the default' is not stated there.

claim: With the balanced only Availability Zone distribution, the group keeps trying to launch in the zone where launches fail instead of moving to another zone; it suits quorum-based workloads and groups that can tolerate losing a zone.
question: When would you choose the balanced only Availability Zone distribution strategy?

values.display: will continue to attempt to launch instances in the Availability Zone

evidence.quote: If launch attempts fail in an Availability Zone, Auto Scaling will continue to attempt to launch instances in the Availability Zone.

This strategy is important to meet certain requirements such as quorum-based workloads or if your Auto Scaling group can tolerate the loss of an Availability Zone because you have sufficient capacity in the remaining Availability Zones.

claim: Since June 30, 2026, the reservations then balanced strategy launches instances into the group's Capacity Reservations first and spreads only the remaining capacity evenly across the enabled Availability Zones.
question: What does the reservations then balanced Availability Zone distribution strategy do, and when was it added?

evidence.quote: Auto Scaling first launches instances into the Capacity Reservations associated with the group, prioritizing reservation use over even distribution across the group's enabled Availability Zones.
After all available reservations are filled, Auto Scaling distributes any remaining capacity evenly across the enabled Availability Zones.

| [Availability Zone distribution: reservations then balanced](#DocumentHistory) | Auto Scaling now provides a **Reservations then balanced** Availability Zone distribution strategy that launches instances into your Capacity Reservations first, and then balances any remaining capacity across Availability Zones. For more information, see [Auto Scaling group Availability Zone distribution](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/autoscaling/ec2/userguide/ec2-auto-scaling-availability-zone-balanced). | June 30, 2026 |

note: NOT EXAMINABLE YET: GA 2026-06-30 is before 2026-07-15 by 15 days, but RULINGS rule 7 treats features GA less than 3 months before the exam as not examinable; label it 'not examinable yet' in the chapter. Demand d18, d60.

claim: Since November 20, 2025, an instance lifecycle policy can keep an instance in a retained state when its termination lifecycle hook ends with ABANDON; without the policy the instance is terminated at once even after ABANDON.
question: What happens to an instance whose termination lifecycle hook is abandoned, with and without an instance lifecycle policy?

evidence.quote: With an instance lifecycle policy configured to retain instances on `TerminateHookAbandon`, the instance moves to a retained state if the termination lifecycle action was completed with `ABANDON` result.
Without an instance lifecycle policy configured, the instance proceeds to termination immediately even if the termination lifecycle action was completed with `ABANDON` result.

| [Instance lifecycle policies](#DocumentHistory) | Instance lifecycle policies give you control over what happens when termination lifecycle hooks don't complete successfully. For more information, see [ Replace root volumes during instance refresh](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/autoscaling/ec2/userguide/instance-lifecycle-policy). | November 20, 2025 |

claim: A retained instance still incurs standard EC2 charges, does not count toward desired capacity (so the group launches a replacement), and must be terminated manually with TerminateInstanceInAutoScalingGroup.
question: Does a retained instance cost money and count toward desired capacity?

values.display: continue to incur standard Amazon EC2 charges
don't count toward your Auto Scaling group's desired capacity

evidence.quote: Instances in retained states continue to incur standard Amazon EC2 charges.
These instances don't count toward your Auto Scaling group's desired capacity, so Auto Scaling launches replacement instances to maintain the desired size.
After you complete the necessary actions on the retained instance, you need to call the `TerminateInstanceInAutoScalingGroup` API to terminate the instance.
